definition: Genial means warm, friendly, and good-humored in manner.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word genial. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know genial should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The genial innkeeper greeted every arriving guest with a broad smile and a cheerful joke about the mountain weather.
A polite host follows the rules of courtesy, while a genial one radiates real warmth and good humor toward each guest.
A genial greeting is warm and friendly, but an effusive one gushes with so much enthusiasm that it can overwhelm the person receiving it.

Affable means friendly and easy to talk to - an approachable manner that puts people quickly at ease. It describes a person's social surface. Genial goes a shade warmer and sunnier: good humor that radiates outward, the joke arriving with the greeting. An affable clerk is easy company; a genial one leaves you smiling on the sidewalk.

Cordial means friendly in a polite, formal way, and it thrives at arm's length - nations keep cordial relations, rivals exchange cordial letters. Genial is warmer and utterly personal: one person's good-humored manner toward the people in front of them. Cordial can be all protocol and no affection; genial is affection you can see on a face.

Genial means warm, friendly, and good-humored in manner.
Customers at the corner barbershop rarely left in a bad mood.
Ortiz, welcomed each person by name, asked about their families, and kept up a stream of gentle jokes while he worked.
Even strangers who wandered in just to ask for directions got a warm greeting and a friendly wave on their way out.
His genial manner made a ten-minute haircut feel like a visit with an old friend.
One person's warm, friendly, good-humored way of treating the people in front of him is exactly what genial describes.

Genial describes one person's manner, expression, or tone in the moment (a genial host, a genial smile, a genial chuckle).
Save it for how an individual treats the people right in front of them, not for the general mood of a party or a place.

Listeners never met Arturo Vega, yet for thirty years they planned their mornings around his voice.
His genial delivery — a chuckle behind the traffic report, a running joke about his own terrible singing — made the drive to work feel companionable.
Colleagues insist the warmth was no performance: he greeted engineers, interns, and janitors with the same delighted grin.
When a flood shut the station for a week, hundreds of listeners wrote in, less worried about the news than about missing a friend.
The station finally printed his rule for new hosts: sound like the morning is good, and mean it.
